summary:
Todd Fisher opens with two formative live experiences: a Slipknot concert whose drum kit rotated vertically mid-solo, and the Broadway production 'Stranger Things: The First Shadow,' whose real-time slow-motion falls looked post-produced. He uses both to argue that engineers should finally tackle their long-deferred side-project list, especially now that AI lowers the build barrier.

He traces the technical lineage of amplified guitar from pickups and speakers through stomp boxes to Peter Frampton's physical-hose talk box. A Halloween tradition of playing guitar while handing out candy led him to dress as Eddie Munson and build a Stranger Things alphabet painter for his garage door, driven by fretted notes. That project raised the next question: how hard could it be to make the guitar speak?

Fisher implemented a JUCE plugin for his DAW, pushing text through Piper and Apple text-to-speech. Saying one word worked. Saying several required automatic word segmentation; energy-gap segmentation failed because running speech often has no silence between words, so he combined it with a sonority-peak syllabifier and finished by manually editing segment boundaries.

For singing, he used the YIN algorithm to read the fundamental frequency off each fretted note, generated a synthesized tone shaped by an ADSR envelope, and routed the voice clip through a vocoder. He then demos chords with the speaking plugin, accepts an audience question ('What is reality?'), and runs the audio through Whisper speech-to-text into a local LLM whose reply is pushed back out through the guitar strings.

For closer-to-singing output, he pre-bakes pitch-shifted samples from the open VocalSet dataset using the World vocoder, because the processing is too heavy to run live. He demos a vowel-only version over backing chords and closes by urging the audience to build their own passion projects, since AI has removed time as the main blocker.

sections.title: Framing and live-performance memories
sections.summary: Fisher introduces himself and his love of guitar, recalls a Slipknot drum solo whose kit rotated to vertical mid-performance, and a Broadway Stranger Things show whose real-time slow-motion falls looked post-produced. He uses both to argue that engineers should finally tackle their long-deferred side-project lists, especially now that AI lowers the build barrier.

sections.title: Lineage from pickups to talk box
sections.summary: He traces guitar sound evolution: pickups plus speakers created rock and roll, stomp boxes added effects chains, and Peter Frampton routed guitar audio through a physical hose into his mouth as the talk box. He notes software emulation now places most effects inside DAWs and asks what the next AI-enabled evolution is.

sections.title: Halloween Eddie Munson costume and garage-door alphabet
sections.summary: Fisher recounts his Halloween tradition of playing guitar for trick-or-treaters, dressing as Eddie Munson, and building a custom app that paints the Stranger Things alphabet on his garage door, driven by notes he plays.

sections.title: Building the JUCE plugin and saying one word
sections.summary: He settles on making his guitar speak, chooses JUCE for a DAW-compatible plugin, and uses Piper plus Apple text-to-speech. The first milestone triggers a single synthesized audio clip on any fretted note, demonstrated live in Logic Pro to applause.

sections.title: Slicing speech into words
sections.summary: Saying several words requires automatic segmentation. Energy-gap segmentation fails because running speech often lacks silence between words. He adds a sonority-peak syllabifier that targets vowels and syllables, then finishes by manually dragging segment boundaries. A demo plays, imperfect but functional.

sections.title: Pitch detection, vocoder, and live jam setup
sections.summary: To make the guitar sing, he uses the YIN algorithm to extract the fundamental frequency of each fretted note, synthesizes a tone with an ADSR envelope, and routes the voice clip through a vocoder as a software talk box. He opens Logic Pro to jam, noting he will not play the title's allusive song because the recording will be posted online.

sections.title: Live chord demo and microphone-driven Q&A
sections.summary: Fisher plays chords on top of a backing track and demos the multi-word speaking plugin after a brief technical-difficulty pause. He then pivots to a conversational variant: a microphone feeds Whisper speech-to-text, the transcript goes into a local LLM, and the LLM's reply is plopped back onto the guitar. An audience member asks 'What is reality?' and the guitar produces an existential answer, which he acknowledges as choppy but working.

sections.title: Pre-baked pitch-shifted VocalSet samples and closer-to-singing demo
sections.summary: To get closer to actual singing, he uses the open VocalSet dataset of recorded singers and the World vocoder to pitch-shift their samples, mapping each fret to a pre-baked vowel sample. Because the process is too heavy to run live, everything is prepared offline. He demos a vowel-only version over backing chords, calls it 'not quite your opera singer, but getting closer,' and invites suggestions for AI-heavier approaches.

sections.title: Closing call to build passion projects
sections.summary: Fisher circles back to his opening charge: what is the audience's passion project? He urges them to build it now that AI removes time as the main blocker, ends with 'be awesome or be good to each other,' and receives applause.

demonstrations: Garage door painted with the Stranger Things alphabet driven by fretted guitar notes via a custom app
JUCE plugin in Logic Pro that plays a single text-to-speech audio clip on any fretted note
Updated JUCE plugin that slices synthesized speech per word, with manually-edited segment boundaries
Live jam of chords with the multi-word speaking plugin overlaid
Microphone-driven Q&A variant where an audience question is transcribed by Whisper, answered by a local LLM, and played back through the guitar
Pre-baked pitch-shifted VocalSet vowel samples mapped to fretted notes and layered over backing chords
limitations: Energy-gap segmentation fails on running speech because there is often no silence between words.
Automatic word segmentation was not reliable enough, so boundaries had to be dragged by hand.
The full pitch-shifted singing pipeline using the World vocoder is too heavy to run live and must be pre-baked.
Live Q&A playback is choppy because speech is still sliced word-by-word rather than sung.
Results are 'not quite your opera singer'; the singing output is closer to vowels than full lyrical singing.

organization.name: Philo Ventures
organization.summary: Philo Ventures is a Utah venture studio that backs and builds companies from pre-idea to first revenue. First-party pages describe Connect, Explore, and Build programs plus first-check capital, with an embedded crew covering design, engineering, go-to-market, legal, and operations. Todd Fisher is listed as Head of Software Engineering on the official team page and is titled that way on the AI Engineer speaker page for this talk. The family site at philo.ventures presents the same firm as a builder across venture and real estate and names Fisher on its people list.
organization.status: Independent Utah venture studio as of the research date. philo.vc homepage, team, and Build program pages are live. No ownership change since the August 2026 talk.
